title: Count, sort, cut: wc, sort, cut, uniq
summary: Four small tools that answer questions about a text file: how many lines, in what order, which column, how often.

text: wc counts. Alone, it gives lines, words and bytes; an option keeps only one of them.
- wc -l is the one you'll use most: how many lines, so how many entries in a list or a log.
- At the end of a pipe, it counts what comes in:
sort prints the lines in order. By default it compares text, character by character, like a dictionary: 10 comes before 2, because 1 comes before 2.
- -n compares numbers, -r reverses the order, -u keeps one of each.
- sort never changes the file: it prints the sorted lines.
cut keeps some columns of each line.
- -d says what separates the columns (the delimiter): -d, for a comma.
- -f says which fields to keep: -f2, or -f1,3 for two of them.
- Columns lined up with several spaces? cut sees empty fields between them: awk handles that better.
These tools are made to be chained with |, one small step each.
- The biggest number: sort -n, then keep the last line.
- How often: sort puts equal lines side by side, uniq -c counts them.
- uniq alone only merges neighbours, so sort first. The lesson on pipes builds a whole chain.
